title: Chemistry of Everyday Life: Food, Medicine, Cleaning

cards.b: Every kitchen, bathroom and medicine cabinet is a chemistry lab. Baking soda, soap, aspirin, preservatives and antiseptics all work by reactions you now know.

• Baking powder and soda: sodium bicarbonate releases CO2 when heated or mixed with acid: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. The gas makes cake and idli batter rise.
  • Maillard browning: sugars and amino acids brown on heat, giving roast flavour.
  • Fermentation: yeast or bacteria turn sugars into gas, alcohol or lactic acid (dahi, idli, bread).

Spoilage comes from microbes and oxidation. Preservation slows them:

  • Salt and sugar pull water out of microbes (osmosis); pickles, jams.
  • Acids (vinegar, lemon) lower pH.
  • Antioxidants (vitamin C) stop fats going rancid.
  • Cold and drying slow reactions.

Food additives: colours, flavours, emulsifiers and preservatives (e.g. sodium benzoate).

Soap is made by saponification: fat + NaOH → soap + glycerol. A soap molecule has a water-loving head and a grease-loving tail. The tails grip oil, the heads face water, forming micelles that wash away.

Detergents are synthetic cleaners that work even in hard water, where soap forms scum with calcium and magnesium ions.

• Analgesics: aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, developed by Bayer, 1897) and paracetamol.
  • Antibiotics: penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, developed as a drug by Florey and Chain around 1940.
  • Antacids: neutralise stomach acid (magnesium hydroxide).
  • Antiseptics on skin and disinfectants on surfaces.
  • Antihistamines: reduce allergies.

Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Misuse breeds resistant bacteria.

Toothpaste uses mild abrasives and fluoride, which strengthens enamel. Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) oxidises stains and kills germs. Never mix bleach with an acid or ammonia-based cleaner, as toxic chlorine or chloramine gas can form.

cards.h: How much acid is in vinegar?
cards.b:
Vinegar is about 5 percent acetic acid by mass. In 200 g of vinegar: 200 x 0.05 = 10 g of acetic acid. Molar mass of CH3COOH = 60 g/mol, so moles = 10 / 60 = 0.167 mol.

Baking soda: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2. 168 g (2 mol, 84 g/mol each) gives 1 mol CO2 = 44 g.

• 'Chemical-free' does not exist. Water is a chemical.
  • Natural does not mean safe (some mushrooms are deadly); synthetic does not mean harmful.
  • Antibiotics do not treat colds (viruses).
  • More soap does not mean cleaner; it is the micelle action that cleans.

Turmeric contains curcumin, a yellow antioxidant studied worldwide. India is often called the 'pharmacy of the world', a leading supplier of generic medicines by volume. Yusuf Hamied of Cipla offered triple-drug HIV therapy at about 350 US dollars per patient per year in 2001, opening access to millions. Hindustan Antibiotics in Pimpri began penicillin production in 1954.

• Baking soda releases CO2; fermentation makes bread, dahi and alcohol.
  • Soap micelles trap grease; detergents work in hard water.
  • Medicines like aspirin and penicillin are targeted organic molecules.

Think about it

1. Why does salting preserve pickles?

2. Why mix soap with water, not oil, to wash oily hands?
